skills.objective: Students use ratio language to describe a relationship between two quantities and generate equivalent ratios by multiplying or dividing both quantities by the same number.
skills.studentObjective: I can describe how two amounts compare and make a new pair of amounts that keeps the same relationship.
skills.languageObjective: I will explain why two ratios are equivalent using because, but and so with the words ratio, for every and equivalent ratios.
successCriteria: I name the order of a ratio and say which quantity comes first.
I make an equivalent ratio by multiplying or dividing both quantities by the same number.
I show the relationship in a table, tape diagram or double number line.
I explain in a full sentence why two ratios describe the same relationship.
skills.bigIdea: A ratio describes a relationship between quantities, and the relationship stays the same when both quantities change by the same factor.

syntax: The ratio of ___ to ___ is ___ to ___.
___ and ___ are equivalent because both quantities were multiplied by ___.
discourse: Compare two batches and justify that they match
Explain why adding the same number changes the relationship

domains.listening: Students listen to a recipe explained aloud and name the ratio and the doubled batch.
domains.speaking: Students tell a partner how they know two batches match and respond to a partner's strategy.
domains.reading: Students read a short recipe passage and underline each quantity and what it measures.
domains.writing: Students write a because, but and so sentence about two equivalent ratios.

vocab.def: A comparison of two quantities that tells how much of one for how much of the other.
vocab.example: 2 cups of blue paint to 3 cups of yellow paint
vocab.nonExample: 2 + 3 = 5, which combines the amounts instead of comparing them
vocab.sentence: The ratio of blue to yellow is 2 to 3.
vocab.morphology: from Latin ratio, meaning reckoning or relation

vocab.def: Ratios that describe the same relationship, found by multiplying or dividing both quantities by the same number.
vocab.example: 2 to 3 and 6 to 9
vocab.nonExample: 2 to 3 and 4 to 5
vocab.sentence: The two batches match because they use equivalent ratios.
vocab.morphology: equi- means equal; valent means worth

vocab.def: A phrase that pairs one amount with another amount again and again.
vocab.example: 3 wheels for every 1 tricycle
vocab.nonExample: 3 wheels and 1 tricycle, with no repeating pattern
vocab.sentence: There are 2 cups of blue for every 3 cups of yellow.

vocab.def: Rows and columns that organize pairs of numbers so you can see a pattern.
vocab.example: A ratio table with blue cups in one column and yellow cups in the other
vocab.nonExample: A table where you eat lunch
vocab.sentence: Mina makes a table to check her batches.
vocab.everyday: A piece of furniture with a flat top and legs

vocab.def: A ratio that compares one part of a group to the whole group.
vocab.example: 2 blue cups to 5 cups of paint in all
vocab.nonExample: 2 blue cups to 3 yellow cups, which compares two parts
vocab.sentence: The part-to-whole ratio of blue to all the paint is 2 to 5.

misconceptions.belief: To make an equivalent ratio, add the same number to both amounts.
misconceptions.why: Students know that adding the same amount to two things keeps the difference, and they treat the ratio as a difference.
misconceptions.fix: Build the batch from copies of the recipe so the pattern is repeated groups, then compare 2 to 3 with 4 to 5 on a double number line.

errorCase.story: Luis wants a bigger batch of the 2 to 3 green paint recipe.
steps: The recipe is 2 cups of blue to 3 cups of yellow.
I want more, so I add 4 to each amount: 2 + 4 = 6 and 3 + 4 = 7.
So 6 to 7 is equivalent to 2 to 3.
errorCase.explain: Adding the same number changes the relationship. Equivalent ratios come from multiplying both quantities by the same number: 2 × 3 = 6 and 3 × 3 = 9, so 6 to 9.

misconceptions.belief: The order of the quantities in a ratio does not matter.
misconceptions.why: Students read a ratio as two numbers instead of as a relationship between named quantities.
misconceptions.fix: Always label each number with its quantity and ask which quantity comes first in the question.

errorCase.story: A class has 3 cats and 5 dogs in a picture book.
steps: There are 3 cats and 5 dogs.
The ratio of dogs to cats is 3 to 5.
errorCase.explain: The ratio of dogs to cats puts dogs first, so it is 5 to 3. The ratio of cats to dogs is 3 to 5.

misconceptions.belief: A ratio of 2 to 3 means 2 out of 3 parts are blue.
misconceptions.why: Students read the ratio as a fraction of the whole instead of a comparison of two parts.
misconceptions.fix: Draw a tape diagram with 2 blue parts and 3 yellow parts, count all 5 parts, and ask what each ratio compares.

errorCase.story: There are 2 cups of blue paint and 3 cups of yellow paint in a mix.
steps: Blue is 2 and yellow is 3.
The mix is 2 out of 3 blue.
So 2/3 of the mix is blue.
errorCase.explain: The ratio 2 to 3 compares blue to yellow. There are 5 cups in all, so blue is 2 out of 5 cups.

misconceptions.belief: '2 for every 3' means the two amounts are the same size.
misconceptions.why: The phrase 'for every' is unfamiliar, so students read it as 'and' or 'each' without a repeated pattern.
misconceptions.fix: Act out 'for every' with counters: place 2 blue, then 3 yellow, then repeat, and say the phrase each time.

reading.title: Mina's Green Paint
reading.text: Mina is painting a mural for the school hallway. She mixes blue paint and yellow paint to make green. Her recipe says to use 2 cups of blue for every 3 cups of yellow. That is a ratio of 2 to 3. Mina needs a lot of green, so she makes the recipe three times. She multiplies both amounts by 3 to keep the relationship the same. Now she uses 6 cups of blue and 9 cups of yellow. Her friend Dev makes a batch with 4 cups of blue and 6 cups of yellow. He says the batches have different amounts, so the greens must be different. Mina builds a table to check. The ratios 2 to 3, 4 to 6, and 6 to 9 are equivalent ratios because each pair has the same relationship. The batches are different sizes, but the color is the same.
reading.simple: Mina is painting a mural. She mixes blue paint and yellow paint to make green. Her recipe uses 2 cups of blue for every 3 cups of yellow. She makes the recipe 3 times. Now she uses 6 cups of blue and 9 cups of yellow. Dev uses 4 cups of blue and 6 cups of yellow. The ratios 2 to 3, 4 to 6, and 6 to 9 are equivalent ratios. They have the same relationship. The batches are different sizes, but the green is the same.

questions.q: How many cups of yellow paint does Mina use after she makes the recipe three times?
questions.a: 9 cups

questions.q: Why can Dev's green match Mina's green even though he uses different amounts?
questions.a: Both batches have the same relationship: each pair is the 2 to 3 recipe made 2 times or 3 times.

questions.q: Is 4 to 6 equivalent to 2 to 3? How do you know?
questions.a: Yes. Both quantities in 2 to 3 were multiplied by 2.

wdntb.why: 5 to 7 is not equivalent to 2 to 3, but the other three are, because each is 2 to 3 multiplied by the same number.

noticeWonder.prompt: Look at the table of blue and yellow cups: 2 and 3, 4 and 6, 6 and 9. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: Multiplying both parts of a ratio by the same number other than zero makes an equivalent ratio.
asn.why: Each quantity changes by the same factor, so the relationship between them stays the same.

asn.claim: A ratio of 3 to 4 and a ratio of 4 to 3 are equivalent.
asn.why: The order is different, so the relationship is different. 3 to 4 would need 4 to be multiplied to become 3.

wyr.q: Would you rather show 2 cups of blue for every 3 cups of yellow with a ratio table or a double number line?

compare.a: Maya doubles both amounts: 2 to 3 becomes 4 to 6.
compare.b: Noah adds 2 to both amounts: 2 to 3 becomes 4 to 5.
compare.prompt: Which strategy keeps the relationship the same? How do you know?

debate.claim: Two batches of paint with different total amounts can still make the same color.
debate.forEvidence: Equivalent ratios like 2 to 3 and 4 to 6 have the same relationship, even though the totals are 5 cups and 10 cups.
debate.againstEvidence: A different amount of blue paint must make a different shade, because 4 cups of blue is more than 2 cups.

listening.script: Listen to Dev explain his smoothie. I use 3 cups of strawberries for every 2 cups of bananas. If I want a bigger batch, I double it. Then I have 6 cups of strawberries and 4 cups of bananas. Notice that I did not add the same number to both. I multiplied both by 2. My friend says she would add 3 to each amount, which makes 6 cups of strawberries and 5 cups of bananas. But then the taste changes, because the relationship changed. A ratio keeps its meaning only when both amounts change by the same factor.

tasks.q: How many cups of bananas are in the doubled batch?
tasks.why: Dev doubles 2 cups of bananas to get 4 cups.

tasks.q: Dev's friend adds 3 to each amount. What is the error?
options: Adding the same number does not keep the relationship the same.
The numbers are too big to add.
Bananas should always come first in the ratio.
tasks.why: Equivalent ratios come from multiplying both quantities by the same factor, not from adding.

story.title: The Mural Mix
story.goal: mix enough green paint for the whole mural
story.intro: Mina has a recipe for green paint: 2 cups of blue for every 3 cups of yellow. The principal asks for a mural twice as long as planned, so Mina needs much more paint.

beats.lead: Mina fills the first bucket and checks the recipe.
beats.success: The first bucket matches the recipe, so Mina's green looks right.
beats.redirect: The green looks a little off, so Mina goes back to the recipe and compares each amount.

beats.lead: Dev offers to mix a second batch and wants to check his plan.
beats.success: Dev's table shows the same relationship, so the two buckets blend perfectly.
beats.redirect: The buckets do not match, so Dev and Mina compare their tables to find the first different step.

beats.lead: The paint shop needs an exact order before it closes.
beats.success: Mina orders the right jars and explains her plan in one clear sentence.
beats.redirect: The order is a little short, so Mina checks how many copies of the recipe she needs.

story.ending: The hallway mural shines in one steady green, and Mina can explain why every batch matches.

panels.says: My recipe uses 2 cups of blue for every 3 cups of yellow.
I need more paint, so I will add 2 cups to each.
Wait. Let us compare 2 to 3 with 4 to 5 on a double number line.
Oh! The relationship changed. I should multiply both amounts by 2.

predict.q: Dev wants twice as much green. Before Mina answers, predict the amounts that keep the same color.
options: 4 cups of blue and 6 cups of yellow
4 cups of blue and 5 cups of yellow
2 cups of blue and 6 cups of yellow
predict.why: Both quantities are multiplied by 2, so 2 to 3 becomes 4 to 6.

transfer.relationship: For every 2 of one quantity there are 3 of the other
phrasings: 2 cups of blue for every 3 cups of yellow
The ratio of blue to yellow is 2 to 3
blue : yellow = 2 : 3
For each 2 cups of blue paint, add 3 cups of yellow paint

decoys.text: The ratio of yellow to blue is 2 to 3
decoys.why: The order is reversed, so this says 2 cups of yellow for every 3 cups of blue.

decoys.text: 2 out of every 3 cups are blue
decoys.why: This compares blue to the whole mix, a part-to-whole ratio, not blue to yellow.

modeling.title: Planning the mural paint
modeling.scenario: A fictional class is painting a hallway mural. The green paint recipe uses 2 cups of blue for every 3 cups of yellow, and the mural needs 30 cups of green paint in all.
assumptions: The cups of blue and yellow add up to the cups of green, with no paint lost.
Every batch uses exactly the recipe amounts.
The mural needs the same shade of green everywhere.
prompts: How many batches of the recipe make 30 cups of green paint?
How many cups of blue and how many cups of yellow should the class buy?
What would change if the mural needed 45 cups of green paint?
limits: Real paint can differ from jar to jar, so the color might not match exactly.
We assumed no paint is wasted or left in the buckets.

sentence.base: The ratios 2 to 3 and 4 to 6 are equivalent.
sentence.because: The ratios 2 to 3 and 4 to 6 are equivalent because both quantities in 2 to 3 were multiplied by 2.
sentence.but: The ratios 2 to 3 and 4 to 6 look different, but they describe the same relationship.
sentence.so: Both quantities were multiplied by 2, so the ratios 2 to 3 and 4 to 6 are equivalent.

diagnostic.prompt: Show 2 cups of blue paint for every 3 cups of yellow paint. Then show a bigger batch with the same green and tell how you know it matches.
lookFor: Multiplies both quantities by the same number
Labels which quantity is which in each pair
Uses a table, tape diagram or double number line correctly
diagnostic.language: Let the student show the bigger batch with a drawing or a table before speaking or writing. If the picture is correct, the barrier is language, not the relationship.

extension.task: Find two ratios that are equivalent to 2 to 3 and one that is not. Use a double number line to show the difference.
extension.reasoning: Write a convincing argument that 5 to 8 is not equivalent to 2 to 3, using multiplication.

en.learning: Your child is learning to compare two amounts with a ratio, like 2 cups of blue paint for every 3 cups of yellow paint.
en.say: To make more of the same, do the same thing to both amounts, like doubling both.
en.ask: If a recipe uses 2 scoops for every 3 cups, how many scoops do we need for 6 cups?
en.activity: Cook together and make a recipe twice. Ask your child to say how much of each ingredient you need, and why.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo a comparar dos cantidades con una razón, como 2 tazas de pintura azul por cada 3 tazas de pintura amarilla.
es.say: Para hacer más de lo mismo, hagan lo mismo con las dos cantidades, por ejemplo, duplicar las dos.
es.ask: Si una receta usa 2 cucharadas por cada 3 tazas, ¿cuántas cucharadas necesitamos para 6 tazas?
es.activity: Cocinen juntos y preparen una receta dos veces. Pidan a su hijo o hija que diga cuánto necesitan de cada ingrediente y por qué.

skills.objective: Students find unit rates from rates given in words, tables and prices, and use them to compare two situations that have different totals.
skills.studentObjective: I can find how much there is for 1 unit and use it to compare two different deals or trips.
skills.languageObjective: I will explain which rate is greater using because, but and so with the words unit rate and per.
successCriteria: I divide the correct quantity by the other quantity to find a unit rate.
I say a rate with its units, such as miles per hour or dollars per notebook.
I compare two situations by comparing their unit rates, not their totals.
I explain my comparison in a complete sentence that names both rates.
skills.bigIdea: A unit rate shows how much of one quantity goes with 1 unit of another quantity, so different situations can be compared fairly.

syntax: ___ miles per hour means ___ miles for each 1 hour.
___ is the better buy because it costs less for each ___.
discourse: Justify a choice between two deals using rates
Explain why a larger total does not mean a greater rate

domains.listening: Students listen to a coach compare two swimmers and name how far each swims in one second.
domains.speaking: Students tell a partner which deal is better and say how they know using the word per.
domains.reading: Students read a trail ride passage and mark each distance, each time and each rate.
domains.writing: Students write a because, but and so sentence that compares two unit rates.

vocab.def: A comparison of two quantities that have different units, such as miles and hours.
vocab.example: 36 miles in 3 hours
vocab.nonExample: 5 miles compared with 3 miles, because both quantities use the same unit
vocab.sentence: Samir's rate tells how far he rides in an hour.
vocab.morphology: from Latin rata, meaning figured or reckoned

vocab.def: A rate that tells how much of one quantity there is for 1 unit of the other.
vocab.example: 12 miles per hour
vocab.nonExample: 36 miles in 3 hours, which is a rate but not a unit rate
vocab.sentence: A unit rate lets us compare two trips fairly.

vocab.def: A small word that means for each, joining two quantities in a rate.
vocab.example: 12 miles per hour
vocab.nonExample: 12 miles and 1 hour, with nothing joining them as a rate
vocab.sentence: The price is $1.20 per notebook.
vocab.morphology: from Latin per, meaning through or for each

vocab.def: A single amount used to measure or count, such as 1 hour or 1 mile.
vocab.example: 1 hour is the unit in miles per hour
vocab.nonExample: Unit 4 of a history book
vocab.everyday: A part of a building, a school course or a larger group, such as an apartment unit
vocab.sentence: A unit rate is the amount for 1 unit.

vocab.def: The cost of 1 item or 1 measure, found by dividing the price by the amount.
vocab.example: $1.20 for 1 notebook
vocab.nonExample: $12 for 10 notebooks, which is a total price
vocab.sentence: Brand B has the lower unit price.

visual.caption: From a total price to a unit price

misconceptions.belief: To find miles per hour, divide the smaller number by the larger number or divide the hours by the miles.
misconceptions.why: Students look for a rule about which number goes first and forget to ask which quantity must be 1.
misconceptions.fix: Ask which quantity should become 1, then use a double number line to show that 3 hours matches 36 miles and 1 hour matches 12 miles.

errorCase.story: Samir rode 36 miles in 3 hours and wants to find his speed in miles per hour.
steps: Miles per hour compares miles to 1 hour.
I divide the smaller number by the larger number: 3 ÷ 36 = 1/12.
So the rate is 1/12 mile per hour.
errorCase.explain: Miles per hour means miles for each 1 hour, so divide the miles by the hours: 36 ÷ 3 = 12 miles per hour. The value 1/12 is hours per mile.

misconceptions.belief: The deal with the smaller total price is always the better buy.
misconceptions.why: Students compare the two prices they see and do not notice that the amounts being bought are different.
misconceptions.fix: Ask what each deal buys, then find the price of 1 item in each deal before comparing.

errorCase.story: Brand A sells 4 notebooks for $6, and Brand B sells 10 notebooks for $12.
steps: Brand A is 4 notebooks for $6. Brand B is 10 notebooks for $12.
Six dollars is less than twelve dollars, so Brand A is the better buy.
errorCase.explain: The amounts are different. Brand A costs $6 ÷ 4 = $1.50 for each notebook, and Brand B costs $12 ÷ 10 = $1.20 for each notebook, so Brand B costs less for each one.

misconceptions.belief: In '12 miles per hour,' the 12 tells how many hours.
misconceptions.why: Students read the number next to a word as a count of that word, and the phrase per hour is unfamiliar.
misconceptions.fix: Say 'for each 1 hour' after the phrase and point to the table row that shows 1 hour and 12 miles.

misconceptions.belief: A unit rate has to be a whole number.
misconceptions.why: Students practice with rates that divide evenly and think the answer must always come out even.
misconceptions.fix: Find the rate for 9 miles in 2 hours on a double number line and read the answer, 4.5 miles per hour.

reading.title: Trail Ride Rates
reading.text: Samir rides his bike along the river trail. In 3 hours he travels 36 miles. To find his unit rate, he divides the distance by the time: 36 ÷ 3 = 12. His rate is 12 miles per hour. A unit rate tells how much of one quantity there is for 1 unit of the other quantity. His cousin Lila rides 45 miles in 5 hours, so her rate is 9 miles per hour. Samir wonders who rides faster. The two riders have a different total distance and a different time, so he compares their rates. Samir rides 12 miles in 1 hour, and Lila rides 9 miles in 1 hour. Samir is faster. A rate makes two different trips easy to compare.
reading.simple: Samir rides his bike 36 miles in 3 hours. He divides 36 by 3 to find his rate: 12 miles per hour. This is a unit rate. It tells the distance for 1 hour. Lila rides 45 miles in 5 hours. Her rate is 9 miles per hour. Samir rides 12 miles in 1 hour. Lila rides 9 miles in 1 hour. Samir is faster. A rate helps us compare two trips.

questions.q: How many miles does Samir ride in 3 hours?
questions.a: 36 miles

questions.q: Why does Samir compare rates instead of total distances?
questions.a: The trips took different amounts of time, so the totals are not a fair comparison. The rates show the distance for 1 hour.

questions.q: Another rider goes 40 miles in 4 hours. Is that rider faster than Lila? How do you know?
questions.a: Yes. 40 ÷ 4 = 10 miles per hour, and Lila rides 9 miles per hour.

wdntb.why: 50 miles in 5 hours is 10 miles per hour. The other three are each 12 miles per hour.

noticeWonder.prompt: Look at two price tags: 4 notebooks for $6 and 10 notebooks for $12. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: A rider who travels more total miles than another rider has the greater unit rate.
asn.why: One rider can go 40 miles in 5 hours, which is 8 miles per hour, while another goes 30 miles in 2 hours, which is 15 miles per hour. The total alone does not decide.

asn.claim: A rider who goes 12 miles per hour and a rider who takes 12 hours per mile move at the same speed.
asn.why: 12 miles in 1 hour is fast, but 12 hours for 1 mile is very slow. The quantities are in a different order.

wyr.q: Would you rather compare two trips with miles per hour or with hours per mile?

compare.a: Dara finds the cost of 1 item: $12 ÷ 10 = $1.20 for each notebook.
compare.b: Eli scales Brand A up to 10 notebooks: 4 × 2.5 = 10 notebooks and $6 × 2.5 = $15, then compares $15 with $12.
compare.prompt: Both compare 4 notebooks for $6 with 10 notebooks for $12. Do both strategies work? Which would you choose?

debate.claim: The best way to compare two prices is to find the price of one item.
debate.forEvidence: A unit price puts both deals on the same footing: $1.50 for one notebook against $1.20 for one notebook.
debate.againstEvidence: Sometimes the package matters more. Buying 10 notebooks when you need 4 wastes money, even if each notebook costs less.

listening.script: Listen to a coach compare two swimmers. Nadia swims 120 meters in 40 seconds. Tomas swims 150 meters in 60 seconds. The coach says, Do not just look at who swam farther. Find the distance for one second. Nadia swims 3 meters each second, because 120 divided by 40 is 3. Tomas swims 2.5 meters each second, because 150 divided by 60 is 2.5. So Nadia is faster, even though Tomas swam a longer distance. The times were different, so only the rates give a fair comparison.

tasks.q: How many meters does Nadia swim in one second?
tasks.why: The coach divides 120 meters by 40 seconds to get 3 meters each second.

tasks.q: A listener says, 'Tomas is faster because he swam 150 meters and Nadia swam only 120.' What is the error?
options: The listener compared the total distances, but the times are different.
The listener should have added 120 and 150.
The listener divided the time by the distance.
tasks.why: The swimmers swam for different lengths of time, so the rates, 3 and 2.5 meters per second, decide who is faster.

story.title: The Market Deals
story.goal: choose the best deals for the class picnic
story.intro: Imani is shopping at the farmers market for the class picnic. Every stall sells food in a different package size, so she cannot just look at the price tags.

beats.lead: At the first stall, Imani compares a small bag and a big bag of apples.
beats.success: Imani finds the price for one apple in each bag and picks the lower price.
beats.redirect: The two bags still look confusing, so Imani writes the price for one apple next to each bag.

beats.lead: At the second stall, a baker sells muffins in boxes of different sizes.
beats.success: Imani compares the cost of one muffin and chooses the box that costs less for each.
beats.redirect: The boxes do not match, so Imani asks what one muffin costs in each box before she decides.

beats.lead: At the last stall, Imani needs to decide how much juice to buy for the whole class.
beats.success: Imani uses the price for one liter to plan how much to buy and explains her choice clearly.
beats.redirect: The total looks too high, so Imani goes back to the price for one liter and checks her work.

story.ending: The picnic table is full, the budget is safe, and Imani can explain each choice with a unit price.

panels.says: One bag has 5 oranges for $4, and the other bag has 10 oranges for $7.
The first bag costs less money, so it is the better deal.
The bags hold different amounts. Let us find the price of one orange in each bag.
Four dollars divided by 5 is $0.80, and seven dollars divided by 10 is $0.70. The bigger bag wins!

predict.q: Imani compares 5 oranges for $4 with 10 oranges for $7. Before she finishes, predict which bag costs less for each orange.
options: The 5-orange bag, because $4 is less than $7
The 10-orange bag, because $7 divided by 10 is less than $4 divided by 5
They cost the same for each orange
predict.why: $4 ÷ 5 = $0.80 and $7 ÷ 10 = $0.70, so the bigger bag costs less for each orange.

transfer.relationship: One quantity changes by a constant amount for each 1 of the other quantity
phrasings: 12 miles per hour
The rider goes 12 miles for each 1 hour
36 miles in 3 hours is the same as 12 miles in 1 hour
d = 12t, where d is miles and t is hours

decoys.why: The order is reversed, so this says it takes 12 hours to go 1 mile.
That is 1 mile for each hour, not 12 miles for each hour.

modeling.title: Choosing a bike rental plan
modeling.scenario: A fictional bike shop offers two rental plans. Plan A costs $15 for 3 hours, and Plan B costs $28 for 5 hours. The numbers are invented for this exercise.
assumptions: The price for each hour stays the same for every hour in a plan.
Both plans include the same bike and helmet.
The renters only care about the cost for each hour.
prompts: Find the cost of one hour with each plan.
Which plan costs less for each hour, and how much less?
Would your choice change if a renter needs only 2 hours? Explain.
limits: Real shops often charge an extra fee for the first hour or for extra time.
A renter may not use every hour of a plan, so the real cost can be different.

sentence.base: Samir's unit rate is 12 miles per hour.
sentence.because: Samir's unit rate is 12 miles per hour because he rides 36 miles in 3 hours and 36 divided by 3 is 12.
sentence.but: Lila rides 45 miles in total, which is more than Samir's 36, but her unit rate is only 9 miles per hour.
sentence.so: Samir rides 12 miles per hour and Lila rides 9 miles per hour, so Samir is the faster rider.

diagnostic.prompt: A store sells 6 pencils for $3 and 10 pencils for $4. Which is the better buy? Show your thinking with a table or a double number line.
lookFor: Finds the price of 1 pencil, or another common amount, for both deals
Labels each number with what it counts, pencils or dollars
Ends with a statement that compares the two deals, not just two numbers
diagnostic.language: Let the student show the comparison with a table or a drawing before speaking or writing. If the table is correct but the sentence is not, the barrier is language, not rates.

extension.task: Find two different packages of juice boxes that both cost $0.75 for each box. Then find a third package that costs less for each box.
extension.reasoning: Explain how you know your third package costs less for each box without comparing the total prices.

en.learning: Your child is learning to find a unit rate, which tells how much there is for 1 of something, like the price of 1 apple or the miles in 1 hour.
en.say: When two deals come in different sizes, find the cost of 1 so you can compare them fairly.
en.ask: A bag of 5 oranges costs $4. How much does 1 orange cost?
en.activity: Next time you shop, pick two packages of the same food and find the price for one item together. Ask your child which is the better buy and why.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo a hallar una tasa unitaria, que dice cuánto hay por cada 1 de algo, como el precio de 1 manzana o las millas en 1 hora.
es.say: Cuando dos ofertas vienen en tamaños distintos, busquen el costo de 1 para compararlas con justicia.
es.ask: Una bolsa de 5 naranjas cuesta $4. ¿Cuánto cuesta 1 naranja?
es.activity: La próxima vez que vayan de compras, elijan dos paquetes del mismo alimento y calculen juntos el precio de uno. Pregunten a su hijo o hija cuál es la mejor compra y por qué.

skills.objective: Students understand a percent as a rate per 100, write a part-to-whole comparison as a percent, and find a percent of a quantity or the whole when the part and the percent are known.
skills.studentObjective: I can write a part out of a whole as a percent and find a percent of a number.
skills.languageObjective: I will explain what a percent means using because, but and so with the words percent, part and whole.
successCriteria: I name the part and the whole before I write a percent.
I rewrite a part out of a whole as an amount out of 100.
I find a percent of a quantity using a tape diagram, a table or benchmark percents.
I explain in a sentence what the percent tells about the part and the whole.
skills.bigIdea: A percent is a rate per 100, so it describes how a part compares with a whole in a way that works for any size of whole.

syntax: ___ out of ___ is the same as ___ out of 100, so ___% of the ___ are ___.
___% of ___ is ___ because ___.
discourse: Describe the part and the whole before giving a percent
Justify why two different groups can have the same percent

domains.listening: Students listen to a gardener describe a plant sale and name the percent that sold.
domains.speaking: Students tell a partner what the part and the whole are and how they know the percent.
domains.reading: Students read a garden passage and underline each part, each whole and each percent.
domains.writing: Students write a because, but and so sentence about a percent and the group it describes.

vocab.def: A rate that compares a part to a whole as an amount out of 100.
vocab.example: 75 out of 100 seeds sprouted, which is 75%
vocab.nonExample: 15 seeds sprouted, which is a count and not a rate per 100
vocab.sentence: A percent shows how a part compares with a whole.
vocab.morphology: per cent comes from Latin and means for each hundred

vocab.def: An amount that belongs to a whole and is compared with it.
vocab.example: 15 sprouted seeds out of 20 planted seeds
vocab.nonExample: A part in a school play
vocab.everyday: A piece of something, or a role in a play
vocab.sentence: The part is 15 seeds.

vocab.def: The complete amount that a part is compared with, which is 100% of the situation.
vocab.example: All 20 seeds planted in the tray
vocab.nonExample: The 15 seeds that sprouted, which are only a part
vocab.everyday: Complete and not broken, as in a whole apple
vocab.sentence: The whole is the 20 seeds in the tray.

vocab.def: A friendly percent, such as 10%, 25% or 50%, that is easy to find with fractions.
vocab.example: 25% is the same as one fourth
vocab.nonExample: 37%, which is not a friendly fraction of a whole
vocab.sentence: A benchmark percent helps me estimate the part.

vocab.def: The part of an amount that matches a given rate per 100.
vocab.example: 25% of 60 seeds is 15 seeds
vocab.nonExample: 25 out of 60, which is a ratio and not a percent of the quantity
vocab.sentence: I found the percent of a quantity with a tape diagram.

misconceptions.belief: If 15 out of 20 seeds sprout, then 15% of the seeds sprouted.
misconceptions.why: Students treat a percent as the number of items in the part instead of a rate per 100.
misconceptions.fix: Build a ratio table that scales the whole from 20 to 100 and watch the part scale with it, from 15 to 75.

errorCase.story: In a tray of 20 seeds, 15 seeds sprout.
steps: The part is 15 seeds and the whole is 20 seeds.
The percent is the part number, so 15% of the seeds sprouted.
errorCase.explain: A percent compares the part with the whole as a rate per 100. Since 15 out of 20 is the same as 75 out of 100, 75% of the seeds sprouted.

misconceptions.belief: To find 25% of 60, divide 60 by 25.
misconceptions.why: Students see the word of and two numbers and pick an operation without asking what 25% means.
misconceptions.fix: Rewrite 25% as 25 out of 100, then as one fourth, and check that the answer is a part smaller than 60.

errorCase.story: Birds might eat 25% of 60 sunflower seeds.
steps: 25% means 25 out of every 100.
I need a part of 60, so I divide 60 by 25: 60 ÷ 25 = 2.4.
About 2 seeds might be eaten.
errorCase.explain: 25% is the same as one fourth, so the part is one fourth of 60: 60 ÷ 4 = 15 seeds. Dividing by 25 does not describe 25 out of 100.

misconceptions.belief: A percent can never be greater than 100%.
misconceptions.why: Students only meet percents that describe a part of a whole, where the part is never larger than the whole.
misconceptions.fix: Compare a plant that is now 30 centimeters tall with its first height of 20 centimeters and read 150% on a tape diagram.

misconceptions.belief: '25% of 60' and '25% more than 60' mean the same amount.
misconceptions.why: The small words of and more than change the whole being compared, but students read both as just a percent and a number.
misconceptions.fix: Draw a tape for each phrase: 25% of 60 is one part of the tape, and 25% more than 60 is the tape plus that part.

reading.title: Ana's Seed Trays
reading.text: Ana's class plants bean seeds in the school garden. In the first tray they plant 20 seeds, and 15 of them sprout. A percent is a rate per 100, so Ana rewrites the ratio of the part to the whole: 15 out of 20 equals 75 out of 100. That means 75% of the seeds sprouted. In a second tray they plant 40 seeds, and 30 sprout. Ana finds that 30 out of 40 is also 75%, so both trays have the same percent even though the numbers are different. Then her teacher says birds might eat 25% of the 60 sunflower seeds in the next bed. Ana knows 25% is one fourth, so she finds one fourth of 60, which is 15 seeds.
reading.simple: Ana's class plants 20 bean seeds in a tray, and 15 sprout. A percent is a rate per 100. 15 out of 20 is the same as 75 out of 100, so 75% sprouted. In another tray they plant 40 seeds, and 30 sprout. That is also 75%. Birds might eat 25% of 60 sunflower seeds. 25% is one fourth. One fourth of 60 is 15 seeds.

questions.q: What percent of the seeds sprouted in the first tray?
Why can a tray of 20 seeds and a tray of 40 seeds both have 75% sprouting?
questions.a: A percent is a rate per 100. 15 out of 20 and 30 out of 40 both equal 75 out of 100.

questions.q: How many sunflower seeds might the birds eat?
questions.a: 15 seeds, because 25% of 60 is one fourth of 60.

wdntb.why: 2/5 is 40%. The other three all name the same amount, 25%.

noticeWonder.prompt: Look at the two trays: 15 of 20 seeds sprouted in one, and 30 of 40 seeds sprouted in the other. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: A percent of a number is always less than the number.
asn.why: 25% of 60 is 15, which is less than 60, but 150% of 60 is 90, which is more than 60.

asn.claim: 50% of any quantity is the same as half of that quantity.
asn.why: 50% means 50 out of 100, and 50 out of 100 is one half.

wyr.q: Would you rather find 25% of 60 with one fourth or with a tape diagram?

compare.a: Lena finds 25% of 60 as one fourth of 60: 60 ÷ 4 = 15.
compare.b: Kofi finds 10% of 60, which is 6, then doubles it for 20%, which is 12, and adds half of 6 for 5%: 12 + 3 = 15.
compare.prompt: Both find 25% of 60. Do both strategies work? Which would you choose and why?

debate.claim: It is fairer to compare two trays by percent than by the number of seeds that sprouted.
debate.forEvidence: A percent puts both trays on a scale of 100: 15 out of 20 and 30 out of 40 are both 75%.
debate.againstEvidence: The number of plants matters too. 30 sprouts give the garden more plants than 15 sprouts, even if the percent is the same.

listening.script: Listen to a gardener describe the plant sale. The club grew 80 tomato plants, and they sold 60 of them. To find the percent sold, I write 60 out of 80. If I divide both numbers by 4, I get 15 out of 20. Then I multiply both numbers by 5, and I get 75 out of 100. So 75% of the plants were sold. The plants left over are 80 minus 60, which is 20 plants. Twenty out of 80 is 25%. The two percents, 75% and 25%, add up to 100%, which is the whole group of plants.

tasks.q: What percent of the plants were sold?
tasks.why: 60 out of 80 equals 75 out of 100, so 75% were sold.

tasks.q: A listener says, '60 plants were sold, so 60% were sold.' What is the error?
options: The percent compares 60 with the 80 plants grown, not with 100.
Sixty is greater than 25, so the percent must be wrong.
The listener should have added 60 and 80.
tasks.why: The whole is 80 plants. 60 out of 80 equals 75 out of 100, so 75% were sold.

story.title: The Spring Plant Sale
story.intro: Joaquín helps run the plant sale at the community garden. Every number he sees, from sold plants to discounts, is easier to understand when he writes it as a percent.

beats.lead: Joaquín counts the plants in the first bed and names the part and the whole.
beats.success: He writes the part out of the whole and turns it into a percent that makes sense.
beats.redirect: The percent looks too small, so Joaquín checks which number is the part and which is the whole.

beats.lead: A neighbor asks Joaquín how many plants a sale of a certain percent would take away.
beats.success: Joaquín finds the percent of the quantity with a tape diagram and answers with a clear sentence.
beats.redirect: The answer is larger than the whole, so Joaquín redraws the tape and finds the part again.

beats.lead: The garden club wants to compare two beds of different sizes.
beats.success: Joaquín compares the two percents and explains that both beds grew equally well.
beats.redirect: The beds still look different, so Joaquín writes each one as an amount out of 100 first.

story.ending: The sale ends with an empty table, a happy club, and a chart where every number is a percent Joaquín can explain.

panels.says: Our bed has 50 plants, and 10 of them are sunflowers.
So the sunflowers are 10%, because 10 is the part number.
Let us compare the part with the whole: 10 out of 50.
Ten out of 50 is the same as 20 out of 100, so the sunflowers are 20%.

predict.q: Joaquín's bed has 50 plants, and 10 are sunflowers. Before Zuri finishes, predict the percent of sunflowers.
predict.why: 10 out of 50 is the same as 20 out of 100, so 20% of the plants are sunflowers.

transfer.relationship: A part compared with its whole as a rate per 100
phrasings: 15 out of 20 seeds sprouted
75 out of every 100 seeds sprouted
75% of the seeds sprouted
The sprouted seeds are 0.75 of the tray

decoys.why: 15 is the part, not the rate per 100. The rate per 100 is 75.
75 is a rate per 100, but this tray has only 20 seeds.

modeling.title: Sorting the seedlings
modeling.scenario: A fictional garden club has 120 seedlings. It plans to sell 75% of them at the spring sale and donate 10% to the school kitchen. The numbers are invented for this exercise.
assumptions: Every seedling is counted once, in only one group.
The sold seedlings and the donated seedlings do not overlap.
No seedlings die before the sale.
prompts: How many seedlings will the club sell?
How many seedlings will the club donate?
What percent and how many seedlings are left?
limits: Real seedlings may not survive until the sale, so the counts could change.
Percents of whole plants are rounded to whole plants, so some counts are only close.

sentence.because: 75% of the seeds sprouted because 15 out of 20 is the same as 75 out of 100.
sentence.but: The two trays have different numbers of seeds, but the percent of sprouted seeds is the same.
sentence.so: Fifteen out of 20 equals 75 out of 100, so 75% of the seeds sprouted.

diagnostic.prompt: In a class of 25 students, 5 walk to school. What percent of the class walks? Show it with a 10-by-10 grid or a double number line.
lookFor: Names 5 as the part and 25 as the whole
Scales the comparison to an amount out of 100
Writes a sentence that names the group the percent describes
diagnostic.language: Let the student shade a 10-by-10 grid or draw a double number line before speaking or writing. If the picture is correct, the barrier is the words part and whole, not percent.

extension.task: Make up a garden problem where 40% of a whole is 24 plants. Find the whole and show how you know.
extension.reasoning: Explain why finding 10% first, by dividing 24 by 4, helps you find the whole.

en.learning: Your child is learning that a percent compares a part to a whole as an amount out of 100, like 75 out of 100 seeds sprouting.
en.say: Percent means out of 100, so 50% is one half and 25% is one fourth.
en.ask: If a $40 shirt is 25% off, how many dollars off is that?
en.activity: At the store, look for a sale sign with a percent. Find the amount off together by using halves and fourths.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo que un porcentaje compara una parte con el total como un número de cada 100, por ejemplo, 75 de cada 100 semillas brotaron.
es.say: Porcentaje significa de cada 100, así que 50% es la mitad y 25% es un cuarto.
es.ask: Si una camisa de $40 tiene 25% de descuento, ¿cuántos dólares se descuentan?
es.activity: En la tienda, busquen un letrero de oferta con un porcentaje. Calculen juntos cuánto se descuenta usando mitades y cuartos.

skills.objective: Students divide fractions by fractions and decimals by decimals, interpret the quotient as how many of one size fit in a total, and check with multiplication.
skills.studentObjective: I can divide fractions and decimals and explain what the answer tells me.
skills.languageObjective: I will explain a quotient using because, but and so with the words quotient, divisor and product.
successCriteria: I tell what the dividend, divisor and quotient are in a division problem.
I use a picture, a tape diagram or a reciprocal to divide a fraction by a fraction.
I divide decimals by changing both numbers in the same way.
I check a quotient by multiplying it by the divisor.
skills.bigIdea: Dividing by a fraction or decimal asks how many pieces of that size fit in the total, and multiplication can check the answer.

syntax: ___ pieces of size ___ fit in ___, so the quotient is ___.
I checked with a product: ___ × ___ = ___.
discourse: Explain what the quotient means in the situation
Justify why both decimals must change in the same way

domains.listening: Students listen to a camp counselor fill cups and bottles and say how many fit.
domains.speaking: Students tell a partner how many pieces fit and how they checked with multiplication.
domains.reading: Students read a ribbon passage and mark the total, the piece size and the quotient.
domains.writing: Students write a because, but and so sentence about a quotient and its check.

vocab.def: The answer to a division problem.
vocab.example: In 3/4 ÷ 1/8 = 6, the quotient is 6
vocab.nonExample: In 3/4 ÷ 1/8 = 6, the number 3/4 is not the quotient
vocab.sentence: The quotient tells how many pieces fit.
vocab.morphology: from Latin quotiens, meaning how many times

vocab.def: The number you divide by, which is the size of each piece or group.
vocab.example: In 3/4 ÷ 1/8, the divisor is 1/8
vocab.nonExample: In 3/4 ÷ 1/8, the number 3/4 is the total, not the divisor
vocab.sentence: The divisor is 1/8 yard.

vocab.def: The fraction you get by switching the numerator and denominator, so the product is 1.
vocab.example: The reciprocal of 1/8 is 8
vocab.nonExample: The opposite of 1/8 is −1/8, which is not its reciprocal
vocab.sentence: I multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor.

vocab.def: The answer to a multiplication problem.
vocab.example: In 6 × 1/8 = 6/8, the product is 6/8
vocab.nonExample: In 6 × 1/8 = 6/8, the number 6 is a factor, not the product
vocab.everyday: Something that is made or grown to be sold, such as a food product
vocab.sentence: I check the quotient with a product.

vocab.def: The dot that separates whole numbers from parts of a whole in a decimal.
vocab.example: The decimal point in 4.5 sits between the 4 and the 5
vocab.nonExample: The comma in 4,500, which separates thousands
vocab.sentence: I move the decimal point one place in both numbers.

misconceptions.belief: To divide fractions, flip the first fraction and multiply.
misconceptions.why: Students remember that something gets flipped but not that the reciprocal belongs to the divisor.
misconceptions.fix: Draw 3/4 as 6 eighths and count how many 1/8 pieces fit, then connect the 6 to 3/4 × 8.

errorCase.story: Keisha wants to find how many 1/8-yard pieces fit in 3/4 of a yard, so she writes 3/4 ÷ 1/8.
steps: Dividing by 1/8 means multiplying by a reciprocal.
I flip the first fraction: 4/3.
4/3 × 1/8 = 4/24 = 1/6, so the quotient is 1/6.
errorCase.explain: The reciprocal belongs to the divisor 1/8, which becomes 8. Then 3/4 × 8 = 24/4 = 6, so six pieces fit.

misconceptions.belief: Dividing always makes a number smaller.
misconceptions.why: Whole number division with small divisors usually gives a smaller answer, so students treat it as a rule for all numbers.
misconceptions.fix: Ask how many pieces of size 1/8 fit in 3/4 and picture many small pieces, which is more than one.

errorCase.story: Keisha has 3/4 of a yard of ribbon and cuts pieces that are 1/8 yard long.
steps: The problem is 3/4 ÷ 1/8.
Division makes numbers smaller, so the answer must be less than 3/4.
3/4 × 1/8 = 3/32, so the quotient is 3/32.
errorCase.explain: Dividing by a fraction less than 1 asks how many small pieces fit, and many small pieces make a larger count. Six pieces of 1/8 fit in 3/4, so the quotient is 6.

misconceptions.belief: To divide decimals, move the decimal point in the divisor only.
misconceptions.why: Students remember that the divisor must become a whole number and forget that the dividend must change too.
misconceptions.fix: Show that 4.5 ÷ 0.9 and 45 ÷ 9 have the same quotient by checking both with multiplication.

errorCase.story: Keisha has a 4.5 meter ribbon and cuts ties that are each 0.9 meter long.
steps: I want to find 4.5 ÷ 0.9.
I multiply only the divisor by 10 so it is whole: 0.9 becomes 9, and I find 4.5 ÷ 9.
4.5 ÷ 9 = 0.5, so the answer is 0.5.
errorCase.explain: Both numbers must be multiplied by 10 to keep the quotient the same, so 4.5 ÷ 0.9 becomes 45 ÷ 9 = 5. Check: 5 × 0.9 = 4.5.

misconceptions.belief: 'Divide 3/4 by 1/8' and 'divide 1/8 by 3/4' mean the same thing.
misconceptions.why: The phrase 'divide a by b' is unfamiliar, and students read the two numbers without noticing which one is split.
misconceptions.fix: Say 'how many 1/8 fit in 3/4' and point to the total and to the piece size, then switch the roles and compare the pictures.

reading.title: Keisha's Ribbon
reading.text: Keisha makes ribbon bookmarks for the library sale. She has 3/4 of a yard of ribbon, and each bookmark uses 1/8 of a yard. The divisor is 1/8, and she wants the quotient of 3/4 ÷ 1/8. She sees that 3/4 equals 6/8, so six pieces fit. She checks with a product: 6 × 1/8 = 6/8, which is 3/4. Her second ribbon is 4.5 meters long, and each tie needs 0.9 meter. To divide, she moves the decimal point one place in both numbers, so the problem becomes 45 ÷ 9. The quotient is 5, so she can cut 5 ties. Moving the point in only one number would change the answer.
reading.simple: Keisha has 3/4 of a yard of ribbon. Each bookmark uses 1/8 of a yard. She finds 3/4 ÷ 1/8. The divisor is 1/8. Since 3/4 equals 6/8, six pieces fit, so the quotient is 6. Her check is a product: 6 × 1/8 = 6/8. Her second ribbon is 4.5 meters, and each tie uses 0.9 meter. She moves the decimal point one place in both numbers and finds 45 ÷ 9 = 5. She can make 5 ties.

questions.q: How many pieces of 1/8 yard fit in 3/4 of a yard?
questions.a: 6 pieces

questions.q: Why does Keisha move the decimal point in both numbers?
questions.a: Multiplying both numbers by 10 keeps the quotient the same and makes the divisor a whole number.

questions.q: How can Keisha check that she can cut 5 ties?
questions.a: 5 × 0.9 = 4.5, which matches the length of the ribbon.

wdntb.why: 3/4 ÷ 8 equals 3/32. The other three each equal 6.

noticeWonder.prompt: Look at the ribbon strips: 3/4 of a yard is cut into pieces that are each 1/8 of a yard long. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: Dividing a positive number by a fraction less than 1 gives a quotient greater than the number you started with.
asn.why: A fraction less than 1 is a small piece, and more than one of those pieces always fit in the number.

asn.claim: The quotient of two decimals has the same number of decimal places as the dividend.
asn.why: 4.5 ÷ 1.8 = 2.5 has one decimal place like 4.5, but 4.5 ÷ 0.9 = 5 has none.

wyr.q: Would you rather divide fractions with a tape diagram or by multiplying by the reciprocal?

compare.a: Ravi draws 3/4 as 6 pieces of 1/8 and counts six pieces.
compare.b: Sofia multiplies 3/4 by the reciprocal of 1/8: 3/4 × 8 = 24/4 = 6.
compare.prompt: Do both strategies find the quotient of 3/4 ÷ 1/8? How are they connected?

debate.claim: To divide decimals, students only need to move the decimal point and do not need to know why it works.
debate.forEvidence: Moving the point gets the right answer fast: 4.5 ÷ 0.9 becomes 45 ÷ 9 = 5.
debate.againstEvidence: Without the reason, students move only one point and get 0.5 instead of 5. A check by multiplication builds the understanding.

listening.script: Listen to a camp counselor explain the drink table. We have 2/3 of a gallon of juice, and each cup holds 1/6 of a gallon. I rewrite 2/3 as 4/6. Four pieces of one sixth fit, so we can fill 4 cups. Then I check: 4 times 1/6 is 4/6, which equals 2/3. Next, we have 6.4 liters of water, and each bottle holds 0.8 liter. I move the decimal point one place in both numbers. Now I divide 64 by 8, and the quotient is 8. We can fill 8 bottles. Notice that I moved the point in both numbers, not just one.

tasks.q: How many cups can the counselor fill with the juice?
tasks.why: 2/3 equals 4/6, so four pieces of 1/6 fit and the counselor fills 4 cups.

tasks.q: A listener says, 'I moved the point only in 0.8, so I divide 6.4 by 8.' What is the error?
options: Both numbers need the same move so the quotient stays the same.
The decimal point should never move.
tasks.why: 6.4 ÷ 8 is only 0.8. Moving both points gives 64 ÷ 8 = 8 bottles.

story.title: The Community Kitchen
story.goal: share food fairly among the volunteers
story.intro: Tomás volunteers in a community kitchen. Every day he cuts, pours and shares food, and the pieces are often fractions or decimals of a whole pan or bottle.

beats.lead: Tomás has part of a pan of cornbread and wants to know how many small servings it makes.
beats.success: Tomás finds how many servings fit and checks the answer with multiplication.
beats.redirect: The number of servings looks too small, so Tomás draws the pan and counts the pieces that fit.

beats.lead: A bottle of juice must be poured into small cups for the lunch line.
beats.success: Tomás moves the decimal point in both numbers and fills exactly the right number of cups.
beats.redirect: The cups do not come out even, so Tomás checks that he changed both numbers in the same way.

beats.lead: The cooks want to split a bag of rice into equal portions for the families.
beats.success: Tomás explains the quotient in a sentence and says what it means for the families.
beats.redirect: The portions look uneven, so Tomás goes back to the divisor and the total and starts again.

story.ending: Every family gets a fair portion, and Tomás can say how many pieces fit and how he checked.

panels.says: A pan has 1/2 of a loaf left, and each sandwich uses 1/4 of a loaf.
Division makes things smaller, so we can make less than half a sandwich.
We are asking how many fourths fit in one half. Picture the loaf.
Two fourths make one half, so we can make 2 sandwiches.

predict.q: A pan has 1/2 of a loaf left and each sandwich uses 1/4 of a loaf. Before Imani answers, predict how many sandwiches Tomás can make.

transfer.relationship: How many pieces of one size fit in a total
phrasings: How many 1/8-yard pieces fit in 3/4 of a yard?
3/4 of a yard is cut into pieces of 1/8 yard each

decoys.why: This multiplies and finds a part of 1/8, not how many 1/8 pieces fit in 3/4.

decoys.text: 3/4 of a yard shared equally into 8 parts
decoys.why: This is 3/4 ÷ 8. Dividing by 8 is not the same as dividing by 1/8.

modeling.title: Bracelet ribbon plan
modeling.scenario: A fictional craft club has a ribbon roll that is 7.5 meters long. It plans to cut bracelet pieces that are each 0.75 meter long, and each bracelet sells for $3.50. The numbers are invented for this exercise.
assumptions: No ribbon is lost when the club cuts it.
Every piece is exactly the same length.
Every bracelet sells at the same price.
prompts: How many bracelet pieces can the club cut from the roll?
How much money would the club earn if it sells every bracelet?
If each piece were 0.5 meter long, how many would fit?
limits: Real cutting wastes a little ribbon, so the club may make fewer pieces.
Not every bracelet may sell, so the money could be less.

sentence.because: 3/4 ÷ 1/8 equals 6 because six pieces of 1/8 fit in 3/4.
sentence.but: Dividing by a fraction less than 1 sounds like making something smaller, but the quotient 6 is greater than 3/4.
sentence.so: Both 4.5 and 0.9 are multiplied by 10, so the problem becomes 45 ÷ 9 and the quotient stays 5.

diagnostic.prompt: Show how many pieces of 1/6 yard you can cut from 2/3 of a yard. Then write the division equation and check it.
lookFor: Draws or names equal-size pieces, sixths, that fit in the total
Writes 2/3 ÷ 1/6 = 4 with the total and the piece size in the right places
Checks with multiplication: 4 × 1/6 = 4/6, which equals 2/3
diagnostic.language: Ask the student to point to the total and to the piece size before writing. If the picture is right but the equation is reversed, the barrier is the phrase 'how many fit in', not fractions.

extension.task: Write a story problem for 3 ÷ 3/5 and solve it. Then explain why the quotient is greater than 3.
extension.reasoning: Use a picture or the product 5 × 3/5 = 3 to justify your answer.

en.learning: Your child is learning to divide fractions and decimals, like finding how many 1/8-yard pieces fit in 3/4 of a yard.
en.say: Dividing asks how many of one size fit into a total.
en.ask: How many 1/4-cup scoops fit in 1 cup? How many fit in 2 cups?
en.activity: While cooking, use a 1/4-cup or 1/2-cup measure to fill a bigger cup. Count the scoops together and write the division.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo a dividir fracciones y decimales, por ejemplo, cuántos pedazos de 1/8 de yarda caben en 3/4 de yarda.
es.say: Dividir pregunta cuántos de un tamaño caben en un total.
es.ask: ¿Cuántas medidas de 1/4 de taza caben en 1 taza? ¿Y en 2 tazas?
es.activity: Cuando cocinen, usen una medida de 1/4 de taza o de 1/2 taza para llenar una taza más grande. Cuenten juntos las medidas y escriban la división.

skills.objective: Students use positive and negative numbers to describe real situations, place them on a number line, compare and order them, find opposites and absolute values, and locate points in all four quadrants.
skills.studentObjective: I can place positive and negative numbers on a number line, compare them, and name points on the coordinate plane.
skills.languageObjective: I will compare rational numbers using because, but and so with the words opposite, absolute value and quadrant.
successCriteria: I place positive and negative numbers in the correct order on a number line.
I name the opposite of a number and its absolute value.
I compare two numbers and say which is greater and why.
I name the quadrant of a point from the signs of its coordinates.
skills.bigIdea: Negative numbers extend the number line to the left of zero, and a number's order depends on its position, while its absolute value tells only its distance from zero.

syntax: ___ is greater than ___ because it is farther to the right on the number line.
The absolute value of ___ is ___ because it is ___ units from zero.
discourse: Compare two negative numbers and justify the order
Explain why two numbers can have the same absolute value

domains.listening: Students listen to a drone dive report and say where the drone is below the ship.
domains.speaking: Students tell a partner which of two temperatures is colder and how the number line shows it.
domains.reading: Students read a weather passage and underline each temperature and each comparison word.
domains.writing: Students write a because, but and so sentence that compares a number with its opposite.

vocab.def: The number the same distance from zero as another number but on the other side.
vocab.example: The opposite of 4 is −4
vocab.nonExample: The reciprocal of 4, which is 1/4
vocab.everyday: Completely different, as in hot and cold are opposites
vocab.sentence: The opposite of −4 is 4.

vocab.def: The distance between a number and zero on the number line.
vocab.example: The absolute value of −4 is 4
vocab.nonExample: −4, which is a position and not a distance
vocab.sentence: The absolute value of −4 is 4 because it is 4 units from zero.

vocab.def: A number that can be written as a fraction of two integers, including negatives and decimals.
vocab.example: −3, 0.5 and 2/3 are rational numbers
vocab.nonExample: A letter or a word, which is not a number
vocab.sentence: A rational number can be negative.
vocab.morphology: from ratio, because the number is a ratio of two integers

vocab.def: One of the four regions the x-axis and y-axis divide the coordinate plane into.
vocab.example: The point (−3, 4) is in Quadrant II
vocab.nonExample: The point (0, 4), which sits on an axis and in no quadrant
vocab.sentence: The point is in the second quadrant.

vocab.def: The point (0, 0) where the x-axis and the y-axis cross.
vocab.example: Every graph on the coordinate plane starts counting from the origin
vocab.nonExample: The point (0, 5), which is on the y-axis but is not where the axes cross
vocab.everyday: The place or moment where something begins
vocab.sentence: Start at the origin and move left 3 units.

misconceptions.belief: A negative number with a larger digit is greater, so −7 is greater than −2.
misconceptions.why: Students use the whole-number rule that larger digits mean larger values and ignore the sign.
misconceptions.fix: Put both numbers on a vertical thermometer and ask which one is warmer, then read the order from left to right on a horizontal line.

errorCase.story: Zara orders the temperatures −7, −2 and 3 from least to greatest.
steps: The temperatures are −7, −2 and 3.
Ignoring the signs, 2 is less than 3 and 3 is less than 7, so the order is −2, 3, −7.
errorCase.explain: On a number line, numbers farther to the left are less. The order from least to greatest is −7, −2, 3.

misconceptions.belief: The absolute value of −6 is −6.
misconceptions.why: Students treat the bars as decoration around the number instead of as a distance.
misconceptions.fix: Count the steps from −6 to 0 on a number line and ask whether a count of steps can be negative.

errorCase.story: Mateo finds how far −6 is from 0 on a number line.
steps: The distance from −6 to 0 is 6 units.
Absolute value is the same as the number, so the absolute value of −6 is −6.
errorCase.explain: Absolute value is a distance, and a distance is never negative. The absolute value of −6 is 6.

misconceptions.belief: Left and up is Quadrant IV.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up the order of the quadrants or the direction each sign points.
misconceptions.fix: Number the quadrants counterclockwise from the upper right and move from the origin with the first number, then the second.

errorCase.story: Zara plots the point (−3, 4) and names its quadrant.
steps: The first number tells the move left or right: −3 means 3 units left.
The second number tells the move up or down: 4 means 4 units up.
Left and up is Quadrant IV.
errorCase.explain: The quadrants are numbered counterclockwise from the upper right. Left and up is Quadrant II. Quadrant IV is right and down.

misconceptions.belief: The opposite of 4 can be any different number, such as 0 or 1/4.
misconceptions.why: In everyday English, opposite means different, but in math it means the same distance from zero on the other side.
misconceptions.fix: Fold the number line at zero and ask which number lands on top of 4.

reading.title: The Weather Station
reading.text: A science class records the temperature at a weather station. At 6 a.m. the thermometer reads −4 degrees Celsius. At 9 a.m. it reads −1 degree, and at noon it reads 3 degrees. Negative numbers are less than zero, so they sit to the left of zero on a number line. The numbers 4 and −4 are opposites because they are the same distance from zero. That distance is the absolute value, so |−4| = 4. Zara says −4 is greater than −1 because 4 is greater than 1. Mateo draws a number line and shows that −1 is to the right of −4, so −1 is greater. Rational numbers include negative numbers, fractions and decimals.
reading.simple: A science class records the temperature. At 6 a.m. it is −4 degrees. At 9 a.m. it is −1 degree. At noon it is 3 degrees. Negative numbers are left of zero on a number line. The numbers 4 and −4 are opposites. They are the same distance from zero. That distance is the absolute value, so |−4| = 4. Zara says −4 is greater than −1 because 4 is greater than 1. Mateo uses a number line. He shows that −1 is to the right of −4, so −1 is greater.

questions.q: What was the temperature at noon?
questions.a: 3 degrees

questions.q: Why is −1 greater than −4 even though 4 is greater than 1?
questions.a: On the number line, −1 is to the right of −4. It is closer to zero, so it is the greater number.

questions.q: What is the opposite of 4, and what is the absolute value of −4?
questions.a: The opposite of 4 is −4, and the absolute value of −4 is 4.

wdntb.why: −5 is the only negative number. The other three are all equal to 5.

noticeWonder.prompt: Look at the thermometer readings: −4, −1 and 3 degrees. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: The absolute value of any number is greater than or equal to zero.
asn.why: Absolute value is a distance from zero, and a distance cannot be negative.

asn.claim: If a number a is less than a number b, then the absolute value of a is less than the absolute value of b.
asn.why: −5 is less than 2, but the absolute value of −5 is 5, which is greater than the absolute value of 2. For 2 and 5, the claim holds.

wyr.q: Would you rather think of negative numbers as temperatures or as money you owe?

compare.a: Mateo uses a number line: −1 is to the right of −4, so −1 is greater.
compare.b: Zara compares the digits: 4 is greater than 1, so −4 is greater.
compare.prompt: Which strategy gives the correct order? What does the number line show that the digits do not?

debate.claim: Absolute value is more useful than the number itself for comparing temperatures.
debate.forEvidence: The absolute values 10 and 2 show how far −10 and −2 are from freezing, which is 0 degrees Celsius.
debate.againstEvidence: To tell which day is colder you need the sign. −10 and 10 have the same absolute value but very different weather.

listening.script: Listen to the report from a research team that sends a small drone below the ship. The ship is at sea level, which we call zero. First the drone dives to −30 meters. Next it dives 20 more meters, so it is at −50 meters. Then it rises 15 meters, so it is at −35 meters. The team says the drone is 35 meters from the ship. That is the absolute value of −35. Notice that −35 is less than −30, even though 35 is greater than 30, because the drone is deeper.

tasks.q: Where is the drone after it rises?
tasks.why: The drone was at −50 meters and rose 15 meters, so it is at −35 meters.

tasks.q: A listener says, '−35 is greater than −30 because 35 is greater than 30.' What is the error?
options: On a number line, −35 is to the left of −30, so it is less.
tasks.why: The drone at −35 meters is deeper than at −30 meters, so −35 is the lesser number.

story.title: Readings on the Mountain
story.goal: record the lowest and highest readings of the week
story.intro: Quinn works at a small research station on a mountain. The instruments report temperatures and heights above and below a marker, so Quinn must read positive and negative numbers carefully.

beats.lead: Quinn lists the morning temperatures and puts them in order on a number line.
beats.success: Quinn places every reading in the right spot and finds the coldest morning.
beats.redirect: The order looks wrong, so Quinn marks each reading on the number line and reads from left to right.

beats.lead: A visiting student asks how far one reading is from freezing.
beats.success: Quinn uses absolute value to find the distance and explains it in one sentence.
beats.redirect: The distance looks negative, so Quinn counts the steps from the reading to zero.

beats.lead: The station plots a weather balloon on a coordinate grid to track where it travels.
beats.success: Quinn names the quadrant from the signs of the coordinates and plots the point correctly.
beats.redirect: The balloon seems to be in the wrong place, so Quinn moves from the origin with the first number, then the second.

story.ending: The weekly report is complete, and Quinn can explain every negative reading with a number line.

panels.says: The thermometer says −8 today, and yesterday it said −3.
Eight is more than three, so today's number is greater.
Let us place both numbers on a number line.
Oh! −8 is farther to the left than −3, so today is colder and −8 is the lesser number.

predict.q: Quinn marks −8 and −3 on a number line. Before Rafael answers, predict which number is greater.
options: −3, because it is farther to the right
They are equal because both are negative
predict.why: On a number line, the number farther to the right is greater, and −3 is to the right of −8.

transfer.relationship: A number and its opposite are the same distance from zero on opposite sides
phrasings: −4 and 4 are opposites
4 is the opposite of −4
Both numbers are 4 units from zero, one on each side
The absolute value of −4 equals the absolute value of 4

decoys.why: 1/4 is the reciprocal of 4. An opposite changes the side of zero, not the size.
Both numbers are on the same side of zero, so they are not opposites.

modeling.title: Reading the station log
modeling.scenario: A fictional mountain station records the temperature in degrees Celsius each morning for five days. The readings are invented for this exercise.
assumptions: Every reading is taken at the same time each morning.
Zero degrees Celsius is the freezing point of water.
A number farther to the left on the number line is a colder temperature.
prompts: Order the five temperatures from least to greatest.
Which day was farthest from 0 degrees, and how far?
How many degrees apart are the warmest and the coldest days? Use a number line.
limits: Real temperatures change during the day, so one reading is not the whole day.
Five days are too few to say what the weather is usually like.

sentence.because: −1 is greater than −4 because it is farther to the right on a number line.
sentence.but: Four is greater than 1, but −4 is less than −1.
sentence.so: The numbers 4 and −4 are the same distance from zero, so they are opposites.

diagnostic.prompt: Place −6, 2, −1 and the opposite of 2 on a number line. Then tell which number is least and how you know.
lookFor: Places −2 as the opposite of 2 on the left of zero
Orders the numbers from left to right as −6, −2, −1, 2
Explains the order by position on the number line, not by the size of digits
diagnostic.language: Let the student place points on a number line before explaining. If the line is correct, the barrier is the words 'less than' and 'opposite', not the numbers.

extension.task: Plot the point (3, −2), its reflection across the x-axis, and its reflection across the y-axis. Give the coordinates of both reflections.
extension.reasoning: Explain what changes in the coordinates when a point is reflected across each axis, and why.

en.learning: Your child is learning about negative numbers, like a temperature of −4 degrees, and how to place them on a number line.
en.say: Zero is in the middle. Numbers to the right are greater, and numbers to the left are less.
en.ask: Which is colder, −6 degrees or −2 degrees? How do you know?
en.activity: Look at the weather forecast or a thermometer together and find a day with a temperature below zero. Draw a number line and mark it.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo sobre los números negativos, como una temperatura de −4 grados, y cómo ubicarlos en una recta numérica.
es.say: El cero está en el medio. Los números a la derecha son mayores y los números a la izquierda son menores.
es.ask: ¿Qué es más frío, −6 grados o −2 grados? ¿Cómo lo saben?
es.activity: Miren el pronóstico del tiempo o un termómetro y busquen un día con una temperatura bajo cero. Dibujen una recta numérica y marquen ese número juntos.

skills.objective: Students write, read and evaluate numerical and algebraic expressions with exponents, and recognize equivalent expressions using the distributive property.
skills.studentObjective: I can write an expression for a situation, find its value, and tell when two expressions are equivalent.
skills.languageObjective: I will explain why two expressions are equivalent using because, but and so with the words expression, variable and coefficient.
successCriteria: I write an expression with a variable for a situation described in words.
I evaluate an expression by replacing the variable with a number and following the order of operations.
I name the coefficient, the variable and the terms in an expression.
I show that two expressions are equivalent using the distributive property or a table of values.
skills.bigIdea: A variable stands for a number that can change, and equivalent expressions have the same value for every number the variable could be.

syntax: The expression ___ means ___ groups of ___ plus ___.
___ and ___ are equivalent because the ___ multiplies both ___.
discourse: Translate a situation into an expression and say what each part means
Justify why two expressions match without testing only one number

domains.listening: Students listen to a volunteer count supplies and match the words to an expression.
domains.speaking: Students tell a partner what each part of an expression stands for in a situation.
domains.reading: Students read a library passage and underline the words that tell groups, amounts and extras.
domains.writing: Students write a because, but and so sentence about two equivalent expressions.

vocab.def: A math phrase with numbers, variables and operations, but no equal sign.
vocab.nonExample: 4c + 12 = 32, which is an equation
vocab.sentence: I wrote an expression for the total number of items.
vocab.morphology: from Latin expressio, meaning a pressing out or showing

vocab.def: A letter that stands for a number that can change.
vocab.example: The letter c in 4c + 12
vocab.nonExample: The number 12, which never changes
vocab.sentence: The variable c stands for the number of books in a bag.

vocab.def: The number multiplied by a variable in a term.
vocab.example: In 4c, the coefficient is 4
vocab.nonExample: In 4c + 12, the 12 is a constant, not a coefficient
vocab.sentence: The coefficient 4 tells how many groups of c.

vocab.def: A number, a variable or a product of both, separated from others by plus or minus.
vocab.example: The expression 4c + 12 has two terms: 4c and 12
vocab.nonExample: The whole expression 4c + 12, which is made of terms
vocab.everyday: A period of time in school, or a word or phrase for something
vocab.sentence: Each term in the expression has its own meaning.

vocab.def: Expressions that have the same value for every number the variable could be.
vocab.nonExample: 4c + 3 and 4c + 12, which differ for every value of c
vocab.sentence: Noor and Eli wrote equivalent expressions.

misconceptions.belief: In 4(c + 3), the 4 multiplies only the first term inside the parentheses.
misconceptions.why: Students copy the pattern of multiplying the number next to the parentheses and stop after the first term.
misconceptions.fix: Use an area model with a 4-by-c rectangle and a 4-by-3 rectangle, so both terms are visible, then test a number.

errorCase.story: Noor rewrites 4(c + 3) without parentheses.
steps: The 4 multiplies everything inside the parentheses.
errorCase.explain: The 4 also multiplies the 3: 4 × 3 = 12, so 4(c + 3) = 4c + 12. A test with c = 2 shows it: 4(2 + 3) = 20, but 4 × 2 + 3 = 11.

misconceptions.belief: In 2 × 3², multiply 2 × 3 first and then square the result.
misconceptions.why: Students work from left to right and forget that an exponent applies only to the number right next to it.
misconceptions.fix: Write 3² as 3 × 3 first, then evaluate the whole expression: 2 × 9.

errorCase.story: Noor evaluates the expression 2 × 3².
steps: The expression is 2 × 3².
I multiply 2 × 3 first to get 6.
errorCase.explain: The exponent applies only to 3, so find 3² = 9 first. Then 2 × 9 = 18.

misconceptions.belief: 3n means 3 + n, or the digits 3 and n side by side like 35.
misconceptions.why: Students read a number and a letter together as addition or as place value instead of as multiplication.
misconceptions.fix: Replace n with 5 and compare: 3n is 3 × 5 = 15, not 8 and not 35.

misconceptions.belief: 'Five less than n' is written 5 − n.
misconceptions.why: Students write the numbers and symbols in the order the words appear, but less than reverses the order.
misconceptions.fix: Replace n with 9 and ask what number is five less than 9, then check which expression gives that number.

errorCase.story: Eli writes an expression for 'five less than a number n'.
steps: The words are five, less than, n, in that order.
I write the numbers in the same order: 5 − n.
errorCase.explain: Five less than n means take 5 away from n, so the expression is n − 5. If n = 9, five less is 4, and 9 − 5 = 4, but 5 − 9 = −4.

reading.title: Packing for the Book Fair
reading.text: The school library is packing bags for a book fair. Each class gets 4 bags, and every bag holds c books plus 3 bookmarks. Noor writes the expression 4(c + 3) to count all the items for one class. Eli counts the books and the bookmarks separately, so he writes 4c + 12. A variable like c stands for a number that can change. In 4c, the number 4 is the coefficient. Noor and Eli test c = 5 books. Noor finds 4(5 + 3) = 32, and Eli finds 4 × 5 + 12 = 32. They try c = 2 and get 20 both times. Their expressions are equivalent expressions because they have the same value for every number.
reading.simple: The library packs bags for a book fair. Each class gets 4 bags. Every bag holds c books and 3 bookmarks. Noor writes the expression 4(c + 3). Eli writes 4c + 12. The letter c is a variable. In 4c, the number 4 is the coefficient. If c = 5, Noor gets 4(5 + 3) = 32 and Eli gets 4 × 5 + 12 = 32. If c = 2, both get 20. The two expressions are equivalent expressions.

questions.q: What does the variable c stand for?
questions.a: The number of books in each bag

questions.q: Why do Noor's and Eli's expressions give the same value for c = 2 and c = 5?
questions.a: Noor counts 4 bags of c books and 3 bookmarks. Eli counts the 4 groups of c and the 4 groups of 3 separately. Both count every item.

questions.q: Find the value of 4c + 12 when c = 6.

wdntb.why: 4c + 3 is not equivalent to the others. The other three are equivalent expressions.

noticeWonder.prompt: Look at the table: when c is 1, 2 and 3, the expression 4(c + 3) gives 16, 20 and 24, and 4c + 12 gives the same values. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: Two expressions that have the same value when c = 2 are always equivalent.
asn.why: c + 2 and 2c both equal 4 when c = 2, but when c = 3 they give 5 and 6.

asn.claim: The expressions 2(x + 5) and 2x + 10 are equivalent.
asn.why: The 2 multiplies both x and 5, so 2(x + 5) = 2x + 10 for every number x.

wyr.q: Would you rather count one bag first or count all the books and then all the bookmarks?

compare.a: Noor thinks of 4 groups of (c + 3): four bags, each with c books and 3 bookmarks.
compare.b: Eli thinks of 4 groups of c books, plus 4 groups of 3 bookmarks.
compare.prompt: Do both ways count the same items? How do you know?

debate.claim: Testing one number is enough to prove that two expressions are equivalent.
debate.forEvidence: If both expressions give 20 when c = 2, they match, and that is a quick check.
debate.againstEvidence: c + 2 and 2c both give 4 when c = 2, but they differ when c = 3. One test cannot prove equivalence.

listening.script: Listen to a volunteer explain how she counts supplies for the library. She says, I fill 3 boxes. Each box gets n pencils and 2 erasers. So the total is 3 times the sum of n and 2. I can write that as 3(n + 2). Now I try n = 4. Four plus 2 is 6, and 3 times 6 is 18. Another way is to count pencils and erasers separately. Three times 4 is 12, and 3 times 2 is 6. Twelve plus 6 is also 18. So 3(n + 2) and 3n + 6 are equivalent expressions.

tasks.q: What is the value of 3(n + 2) when n = 4?
tasks.why: Four plus 2 is 6, and 3 times 6 is 18.

tasks.q: Which expression is equivalent to 3(n + 2)?
tasks.why: The 3 multiplies both n and 2, so 3(n + 2) = 3n + 6.

story.title: The Park Cleanup Plan
story.goal: plan supplies for the park cleanup
story.intro: Priya is organizing a park cleanup. The number of volunteers can change from day to day, so she writes expressions that work for any number of volunteers.

beats.lead: Priya decides how many bags each volunteer will carry and how many spare bags to bring.
beats.success: Priya writes an expression with a variable and says what each part stands for.
beats.redirect: The expression does not match the plan, so Priya reads the situation again and decides which part repeats.

beats.lead: A friend suggests a different way to write the same plan.
beats.success: Priya tests both expressions with two numbers and uses the distributive property to explain they match.
beats.redirect: The two expressions give different values, so Priya checks whether the number multiplies every term.

beats.lead: On the day of the cleanup, more volunteers arrive than expected.
beats.success: Priya evaluates the expression with the new number and counts out exactly enough bags.
beats.redirect: The count looks too low, so Priya follows the order of operations again and finds the slip.

story.ending: The park is spotless, and Priya can explain how one expression covers any number of volunteers.

panels.says: Each of v volunteers carries 2 bags, and I will also bring 6 spare bags.
So the number of bags is 2 + v + 6?
The 2 bags go with each volunteer, so I multiply. The expression is 2v + 6.
With 10 volunteers, that is 2 × 10 + 6 = 26 bags.
